scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: After the killing of Abu Sayed on 16 July, the government shifted from a defensive posture to a nationwide one. On 18 July 2024, internet and mobile-data services were shut down across the country. A curfew was imposed, and the army, the Rapid Action Battalion, and the Border Guard Bangladesh were deployed alongside the police. Multiple outlets described the curfew as shoot-on-sight.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: On 19 and 20 July the toll escalated sharply. Reports at the time placed the death count well above one hundred across those two days, with police fire cited as the cause of more than half of the deaths reported in that window; these figures are approximate and were revised as the situation continued. Protesters stormed a jail in Narsingdi district and set fire to the state broadcaster's Dhaka offices — events that fed into the government's decision to harden its response.

evidence.title: The Curfew and the Blackout
evidence.sourceCaption: As reported by Reuters and Context News reporting on the 18 July 2024 measures.
evidence.text: On 18 July 2024, the government imposed a nationwide internet and mobile-data shutdown and declared a curfew. The army, the Rapid Action Battalion, and the Border Guard Bangladesh were deployed alongside the police to enforce the order. Multiple outlets described the curfew as shoot-on-sight. Mobile data would not be restored for days; broadband would return in stages beginning around 24 July.

evidence.text: The Daily Star's Saturday, July 20, 2024 edition reports on the severe escalation of violence across the country on Friday, July 19, 2024. Coverage highlights army deployment with 'shoot at sight' orders, air deployment of sound grenades and tear gas via RAB helicopters, and damage to major state infrastructure including Metro Rail stations and Setu Bhaban. The paper also outlines emergency situations across major Dhaka hospitals including Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).

evidence.title: High Court dismisses writ petition challenging the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973
evidence.sourceCaption: Bangladesh High Court ruling on the writ petition filed by Supreme Court senior lawyer Muhammad Mohsin Rashid challenging the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973 and the ongoing trials for crimes against humanity linked to the July uprising. Image reference: highCourt.jpg.
evidence.archiveNote: A photograph of the High Court building — the venue for the ruling dismissing the writ petition that challenged the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973. The petition had sought repeal of the act and argued that the trials were being used as a tool to target political opponents.
evidence.text:
The Bangladesh High Court recently dismissed a writ petition challenging the validity of the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act of 1973 and the ongoing trials for crimes against humanity linked to the July uprising. The petition, filed by Supreme Court senior lawyer Muhammad Mohsin Rashid, sought a directive for the government to repeal the act entirely, arguing that the legislation had become obsolete and inoperative following historical developments like the Shimla and Tripartite Delhi agreements. Furthermore, the petitioner contended that the law was being used as a tool to target political opponents and argued that appointing High Court judges to the International Crimes Tribunal violated constitutional provisions regarding judicial independence.

By dismissing the petition, the High Court bench, comprising Justice Khizir Ahmed Choudhury and Justice Md Ziaul Hoque, upheld the legal framework governing these proceedings. This ruling clears the legal path for the tribunal to continue hearing cases related to human rights abuses and crimes against humanity steming from the July uprising, reinforcing the state's mandate to pursue judicial accountability under the 1973 framework.
